text: You can't read amplitudes out of a quantum computer directly — you only ever get classical bits back, one probabilistic sample at a time. The rule connecting the two is the Born rule, and it's the single most computationally consequential equation in this course.

For psi equals a ket-zero plus b ket-one, the Born rule says: the probability of measuring 0 is the magnitude of a squared, and the probability of measuring 1 is the magnitude of b squared. Take 0.6 ket-zero plus 0.8 ket-one: P of 0 is 0.6 squared, 0.36; P of 1 is 0.8 squared, 0.64; and they sum to exactly 1, confirming it's a legitimate state. Measuring this qubit gives 0 about 36% of the time and 1 about 64% of the time, over many repeated identical preparations.

Now take ket-plus, both amplitudes 1 over root 2. The Born rule gives P of 0 equal to 0.5 and P of 1 equal to 0.5 — a perfect even split. Here's the subtle part: ket-minus gives the exact same 50/50 split in the computational basis, even though it's clearly a different state — Hadamard sends ket-plus to ket-zero but ket-minus to ket-one. Measurement statistics in one basis alone don't always tell you the full story.

This is where the Born rule becomes an engineering fact, not just a physics fact. A real circuit builds up a rich vector of amplitudes across every possible bitstring, but when it ends and you measure, hardware doesn't hand you that vector — it hands you exactly one classical bitstring, sampled according to the Born rule. Want an amplitude? You have to run the whole circuit many times and build a probability histogram, and even then you only recover probabilities, never the original phases.

Because you only get one-shot probabilistic samples out, every quantum algorithm is designed around one central goal: push the probability of the correct answer as close to 1, and everything else as close to 0, as the circuit allows. That's exactly the job interference does — wrong-answer amplitudes cancel, the right one grows. Get the circuit design wrong, and you'll sample the right answer only rarely, no matter how elegant the intermediate math was.
Next lesson covers what happens to the qubit the instant after you measure it — collapse, and why it's a one-way door.
